> Forward: @OldBammen Down: also talk about cash flow depreciation: The seniors of the street have a good discussion about cash flow liquidity, and I will talk about some of their own experiences: cash flow is theoretically strict, but in practice there are a lot of limitations, and slightly different assumptions about future profitability, growth or discounting make the final result very different. Like democracy, cash flow is not a good system, but we are not much better. Personally, to use this method, the target firm must be very competitive, and most firms will be competitive until it dies, which is economic law, and it is totally meaningless to predict the future decades of profits of such an enterprise and then to use cash flow liquidity.Second, the security margin must be large, because the method itself is inaccurate, leaving space for itself large. For example, the following is an analysis of data on Coca-Cola purchases by Old Bar in 1988: Cola was purchased at $14.8 Billion, which was almost at the market price of 4-5 and was never cheap from the point of view of traditional value investments. Co-Cola's profit was $828 Million, assuming that it grew at 15 per cent per year from 88 (from 1981 to 1988 it grew at 17.8 per cent per year) and then slowed to 5 per cent per year.Using 9% discount, the Present Value of Coca 1988 should be 48.3 Billion. It's more than three times the old Bar. If you think that the assumptions are too optimistic, let's assume that Coca-Cola has increased its profits by 5% per year since 88, and even on such conservative assumptions, the Present Value has $20.7 Billion, which is 30% larger than the old Bar. So old Bar says he wonders why someone thought that Coca-Cola was valuable at the time, that cash flow was used with caution, and that it was used to emphasize core competitiveness and security margins.

Future cash flow discounts are not formulas, they are ways of thinking. / @flyingsword: I never use cash flow to discount, too complicated and not good, and the formula forgets/ / @sword: I have a style for @swordsway invisible

## 881. 2012-05-15 11:48

But, by contrast, Peter Lynch held a very large stock, and he bought more than 1400 shares when he was in charge of the Magellan Fuda fund. His argument is relatively simple: assuming that you hold an average of 10 stocks, six of them making money, you can basically be at the same level as the big market, and if you have a ten-fold share (Tenbagger), you'll be able to make a big profit. Because the biggest loss of a stock is 100% (i.e., the probability is small), but the rise of a stock is five times more than it can make, 10 times more than it is.The Buffett strategy focuses on the very precise view of each stock, which is difficult for ordinary people to achieve, but Peter Lynch’s strategy, which allows for a few shares to pay for as long as most of your stock earns, is more appropriate for ordinary investors. Of course, they all share the common denominator, that they invest with great caution, and that they fully study and re-invest; and that is, patience.

## 1051. 2012-08-14 09:20

> Forward: @I am JUNG: What should we expect in return? (Recently from Beijing, I wanted to send a new savings campaign (5), and by chance, an article from the “Save for a sword” which I saw in the cold, and which I felt should first present some personal observations on the issue, and if there were any errors, in the hope of being corrected by the brother and everyone in time.) The annual compound growth rate of our GDP: (i) for the last years, 1977-2011.15 per cent 1978-2011.15 per cent 1979-2011:16.1 per cent 1980-2011:16.15 per cent 1981-2011:16.45 per cent (ii) rolling for the 20 years (1977-2011) was a minimum of 1989-2009:16.18 per cent and a maximum of 1977-1999.8 per cent (1997-2011)7:17.38% – so we can conclude that our GDP has grown at about 16% over the past 30 years. So, can we use this increase as a benchmark for expectations or comparisons of returns on the stock market? (iii) 10 years rolling (1991-2011) 17.44%, 16.15%, 14.41%, 12.74%, 11.77%, 11.76%, 12.90%, 14.03%, 14.28%, 14.98%, 15.70%. — If we use historical data only as the central basis of the valuation, then which of the data we give above? If I choose, I would be somewhat confused.More importantly, stock market valuations reflect not only historical truth but also expectations of future growth, so how fast will our GDP grow over the next 10, 20, 30 or more years? If we simply link our stock market valuation hub to GDP growth over the past 20 or 30 years — that is, around 16 per cent — and thus produce a reasonable market surplus of 6.25 times, it means that our return expectations or reference criteria for the stock market over the past 20 years are 16 per cent.Is this a reliable return expectation? The 1991-2011 report indicates a composite annual return (rolling for 10 years): the highest (1991-2001): 18.85 per cent lowest (2001-2011): 2.94 per cent mean: 8.39 per cent median: 6.93 per cent — if we have a 16 per cent return expectation, the above data tells us that most of the returns are very disappointing, except for a few years. Okay, our stock market has a short history and has a PE in the bush, and we will refer to a few sets of data from the United States.(i) In 1866-1922 (source: General Shares for Long-Term Investments) we obtained the following data (all of which are composite returns for more than 10 years) in 12 empirical studies conducted by Edgar Smith: Minimum return: 3.66 per cent of the highest return: 6.59 per cent mean return: 5.31 per cent of the above returns were not included in cash dividends and equity dividends (the demand in the empirical study for the sale of all red shares) and, subject to a 50 per cent reinvestment rate, we could roughly revise the above average data to around 10-12 per cent. 1866-1922 was the period when the United States was transformed into the world ' s largest economy, and we saw that stock returns for this period remained at roughly 10-12 per cent.(ii) Major phases of the twentieth century (source of data: The Power of the Chiefs of the Share: 1802-1870 (United States from agro-social to industrial as the economic mainstay): 7.1 per cent, 1871-1925 (United States development into the world's first political and economic power during this period): 7.2 per cent, 1926-2006 (United States time as a standard for assessing returns to its stock market): 10.1 per cent 1946-1965 (post-war 20 years): 13.1 per cent 1946-2006 (post-war 60 years): 11.2 per cent 1966-1981 (stock market from cattle to bear): 6.6 per cent 1982-1999 (from Bear to Century Bull): 17.3 per cent — is the so-called 16 per cent middle of the valuation, or is the return expected to be somewhat optimistic, when compared with United States data?Since the US stock market returns also include increases and decreases in the market rate, let's look at a set of historical data on the growth of profits in enterprises (Information: Investor Future): (i) the growth rate of profits per share of 20 “best survivors” of the standard 500 components (1957-2003),1 above 14 per cent: 1; 2 above 10 per cent: 7; the rest: 6.2 per cent - 9.82 per cent - do we really believe that the earnings of our listed companies (indexed shares) will grow at an average rate of 16 per cent?We already know that the United States stock market surplus has fluctuated around 10-20 times over the past 100 years, with only two declines below 10 times, in 1920 and around 1981. The two major declines in the market rate were accompanied by a sharp depreciation of the dollar, with US interest rates on long-debted debt rising by 16% in 1980. By contrast, while our consumer price index has been positive for many years, long-debt interest rates will not be adjusted to 16%, and how the average market surplus will (or need) fall below 10 times as much as the US?If the market surplus is required to be adjusted to 6.25 times (the return is expected to be 16 per cent), what is the level of the premium on equities at more than 10 points in relation to inflation and long debt (we do not consider the 93-95 situation as a normal situation)? From the data set given below, we can see a slight indication: stock premiums (as opposed to long-debt) in the major Western markets (1900-2000): Germany: 7.1; Japan: 6.6; Australia: 5.9; Italy: 5.0; Sweden: 5.0; United States: 4.9; France: 4.8; United Kingdom: 4.8; Canada: 4.7; Netherlands: 4.2; Switzerland: 2.4; Denmark: 1.9. Of course, we can say that the return on our fixed-income financial instruments is distorted.However, we have calculated the relationship between our five-year bank periodic savings returns and inflation over the past 20 years, which is on average only 1-2 points short of the Western market, minus the above-mentioned premium of 7-8 points for the required returns on stocks against the risk-free rate of return. Perhaps this time we will be speaking, and then we will be more practical: Manger says: Reducing your expectations is the smartest move. Now let us interpret this statement with an investment example: in mid-July 2005, the pup is traded at around $52, and the static and dynamic PE are 23.93 and 20.96 times more than the respective prices.We now have two models of analysis and decision-making: the GDP model, which has been 16.76% of our annual composite GDP growth in 1984-2004, with a reasonable 5.97% of the calculated PE. The annual compound gains per share in the huts increased by 33.64% and 34.40%, respectively, in 2001-2004 and 2001-2005, thus giving us a figure of about two times the GDP per share, while the market surplus on the stock was 3.51-4.01 times the fair market surplus. Should we buy the stock in the hut?2. The Buffett model, one of which calculated the return on investment in 2005 as the 2005 dynamic PE, would have been 4.77%. If Mao had increased at 15% over the next 10 years (which was not an overly optimistic projection at the time), the return would have been $10.03 per share after 10 years, and the original return on investment would have been 19.28% (not counting dividends). If he continued to hold it, the return on the original investment would have been higher.In fact, the annual compound returns on stocks in 2005-2012 were almost hundreds of times higher than double-digits, and the Poo station was not the most rewarding. Those who bought good listed company shares in 2005 (including 2002-2004) and held them until today, he/she should know what I was saying. 80 years ago, Graham had made people lower their stock-buying rates because of concerns about economic prospects, and today's Cold Brother had his/her market-buying rates cut because he had a good economic outlook (assuming we were back at the point where we were a few years or ten years ago).

Let's say our own expectations of returns; first, I never anticipate returns because returns on investments are not inherently related to my expectations. My understanding of investments is that processes are more important than outcomes, or that schemes are in the right place, and the results are always better. Second, running through bank deposits is the most basic requirement in the long term, or what is the rush. Third, from a value-saving perspective, returns on investments are not bad if they are at least as good as they are in the long term as they are in the purchasing power, perhaps it is interesting to measure with gold.

Source:https://xueqiu.com/1247347556/22111728

The discount rate used for valuation is not the expected rate of return, but the required rate of return. The required rate of return is a comparison with opportunity costs.

## 5908. 2023-07-22 06:59

> Forward: @HUNHUNDIEant: Monish Pabley: I have a challenge for my web link to invest in China. I usually tell my friend Li-shu, if I want to invest in China, what is reasonable and what is not. Li suggested me buy the poo-shut a few years ago, and I did it, and it was a lot higher, but it was really nice. A few years later, I visited China's Mau-sakry with my daughter and friend Gay Spiel, and it was wonderful, and it was an incredible company. So I think China has a lot of great businesses and a lot of great opportunities. Chinese people are probably easier to screen all this information than I am. But if someone like Li-shue helped me, it would be very smooth.He said to me, "Monish, you bought the poohouse?" He said, "Yes." He said, "You know that even if you weren't there, the poohouse was still there?" I said, "Yes." So the situation was God told me, "No poo-pots ever, okay?" Charlie Munger was God of the investment community, and God told me, "No poo-stock shares ever." So I said, "I never intended to sell." And after a few years, Lee called me, "I'm selling the pony stock, and I think you should sell it." I said, "But God told me never to sell it." He said, "Well, he found some problems in the poo-pock sale, perhaps corruption in the marketing process, which bothers him. He said, "I think you should sell it and then continue investing in other projects."And I thought and said, "I don't know anything about Mao Dai, I don't even drink, Li Su-sang knows anything." So I said, "I've made five or six times what I think I should listen to him." So I sold the stock I never intended to sell. After a few years, the price doubled and went up. My daughter also invested in the table, and when I told her about it, she said, "I don't sell it." Because she liked the company and she liked to visit the view of the town. I was stupid enough to sell it.

Mohnish can't make a concentrated investment, because he has a ceiling of 10%. We used to meet him a few years ago, and I told him about apples in 2011-2012, but he couldn't listen. He thinks Mangbi Barfit is good, which I disagree with (there's no disrespect for Mang, he's a very rare, intelligent man). It's hard to understand people who want to see anything else after they've read it. In 2014, I wanted to talk to him about apples, but Mohnish said they would never be interested. Although I didn't say it because I made a final decision (and I'm a little embarrassed because I already bought a lot), he said something that affected me a little bit.And Mr. Barfite bought apples in 2016, and when I met Barbas in 2018, I mentioned that I wanted to talk to him about apples in 2014, but I didn't mean it. Ba was “very harsh” criticizing me, saying that he would not hesitate to tell him about it next time.

Here are some more effective ways of guiding and hoping to help you: 1. Understanding the reasons behind the behaviour of the child: Age characteristics: Young children may be more vague about the concept of time and less self-management capacity, so they can be vulnerable to drag. • Attention: Some children may be distracted by other things, which may lead to delays. • Emotional problems: Children may be delayed by anxiety, fear or conflict. • Family environment: If parents are generally less demanding on time management, children may also become involved in drag.• To help children to develop reasonable schedules for their children to develop their own habits; • To warn them before important events occur, to give them adequate time to prepare for them; • To break down tasks: to make it easier for children to take action by dividing them into small, easy-to-do parts; • To encourage: to give recognition and encouragement in time when they show progress, and to enhance their self-confidence; • To develop the idea of time: to help children understand the concept of time by playing games, drawing books, etc. • To control emotions: When a child is dragged, parents must try to control their emotions and avoid scolding them. • To be a good example for parents: to be good examples for children.3. Addressing the problem of late arrival: working with the child to analyze the reasons for late arrival, whether it is late to get up, leave the house or be late on the road. • Developing solutions: working out solutions with the child, depending on the reasons for late arrival, such as getting ready for clothes to wear the following day, setting alarm clocks, etc. • Taking consequences: late arrival because of drag, leaving the child with the consequences, such as being criticized by the teacher, missing the activity, etc. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .Other recommendations — Patience: steering children to change their drag habits takes time and patience, and does not expect to be done at once. • Communication: maintaining good communication with children and understanding of their thoughts and feelings. • Seek professional help: If the problems of children are serious, you can ask professional help. Remember: every child is unique and the approach appropriate to others is not necessarily appropriate for your children.

## 7533. 2024-09-15 07:19

> Forward Original: @Lianghong: A wave of the Bounty Weibo's base is a wave of customs bottoms and this base is solid

First, it reflects the core idea of Buffett's value investment that investors should think about investment as the owner of the business. He argues that stock represents part of the ownership of the company and that investment stock is essentially an investment company. So, when investors buy stock, they should evaluate its value as if they were the company. Secondly, it also stresses the importance of companies buying their own shares at a price lower than their intrinsic value.In this case, the company is actually buying its own shares with its own cash flow, which can reduce the number of shares in circulation and raise each share of the proceeds, thereby potentially driving up the price of the stock. Moreover, Buffett’s statement may mean that, in the long run, the company’s intrinsic value will eventually be reflected in the price of the stock. If the company can continuously create free cash flows and make effective use of those cash, whether through dividends, reinvestment or buybacks, it can add value to the company and eventually attract investors to purchase its stock.This investment concept is consistent with Buffett’s consistent long-term, value-based and concentrated strategy. This is the answer to the Kimi model. Is it true that the Boulevard is right?

Blood donation takes a different time to recover from humans, but generally most people recover after blood donation: blood capacity is restored: blood donation is lost mainly from about 200 to 400 milligrams of blood (the amount depends on the type of blood donation). Normally, blood capacity recovery takes about 24 to 48 hours. During this period, the body recovers blood capacity by replenishing liquids. Red cell recovery: red cells recovers relatively long, usually four to six weeks, depending on the individual ' s health and nutritional status. Blood protein (the material transporting oxygen in blood) also needs some time to recover.Blood plasma recovery: plasma (liquid composition in blood) recovers faster than red cells, usually returning to normal levels within 24-48 hours. Iron restoration: after blood donation, iron reserves are reduced, as iron is an important ingredient for synthetic red cells. Recovery of iron usually takes weeks to months, and some may need to accelerate recovery by replenishing iron or eating more iron-rich food (e.g. red meat, spinach, etc.). Recommendations during recovery: Multi-water: after giving blood, ensure that it is adequately replenished and the blood is restored. Due rest: avoids intense movement and overwork. Dietling: increase foods rich in iron, protein, vitamin B12 and folic acid, and helps to improve the body ' s recovery. Avoid drinking: it is best to avoid drinking alcohol after giving blood, and avoid any impact recovery.Overall, if you feel that you are not sick, that you have a proper rest and diet, most people can recover completely from the pre-blood donation state within days to weeks, but the recovery of red cells and iron may take longer. DeepSeek, like many AI and Deep learning companies, likely relies on **Nvidias CUDA** for GPU acceleration, given its widespread adoption in the industry. Heres a breakdown of why:1. **GPU Dependency**: Training large AI models typically requires powerful GPUs. Nvidias GPUs (e.g., A100, H100) dominate this space, and CUDA is the primary platform for optimizing computations on these GPUs.2. **Frameworks and Libraries**: Popular deep learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow) are built on CUDA for GPU acceleration. Unless DeepSeek uses custom alternatives, they likely depend on these CUDA-optimized tools.3. **Cloud Infrastructure**: If DeepSeek uses cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP), their GPU instances are predominantly Nvidia-based, requiring CUDA for efficient computation.4. **Ecosystem Lock-In**: The deep learning ecosystem heavily favors CUDA due to compatibility with libraries (cuDNN, NCCL) and pre-trained models. Switching to alternatives like AMD ROCm would involve significant effort and potential performance trade-offs.**Exceptions**: If DeepSeek uses custom hardware (e.g., TPU-like accelerators) or prioritizes non-Nvidia solutions, they might reduce CUDA dependency. However, theres no public evidence of this.**In short**, while specific internal infrastructure details arent public, its highly probable that DeepSeek depends on CUDA for GPU-accelerated AI workloads, as do most companies in the field.

Pont Julien (Julican Bridge) is an ancient Roman arch bridge on the Karaon River in south-eastern France, built three years B.C., which is a key traffic project on the Roman Empire ' s important road, Via Domitia. The bridge is located five kilometres north of Bonnieux in the Provence area, near the Apt city. The bridge is approximately 85 metres long and 5.5 metres wide, consisting of three arches, with a maximum distance of 16.3 metres, all constructed using finely cut limestone, without the need for a patch of dust. The bridge is high in shape and is relatively low on both sides. The bridge is specially designed for flooding seasons.The bridge, which has been used continuously since its construction for nearly 2,000 years, has been responsible for important regional traffic until 2005 when motor traffic was closed to protect the ancient bridge structure, which is now mainly for walking and riding. Pont Julien has not only demonstrated the remarkable bridge building technology of ancient Rome, but also witnessed the profound impact of the Roma network on Western Europe for thousands of years.
